title: Relationship Visualization
learning_outcomes: Explain relationship visualization and accurately refer to at least two syllabus subtopics.
Apply the main idea of relationship visualization to a small example, trace, calculation, or scenario.
Identify one important assumption or failure mode and describe how to check it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study relationship visualization in the context of data visualization and storytelling. You will connect the PDF subtopics to a small example and practice describing what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Relationship Visualization matters because it affects how data is collected, represented, analyzed, interpreted, or used in a decision. Check the task and assumptions before choosing a method.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: A visualization encodes values using position, length, area, color, and other channels. The chart type, axis, units, ordering, and annotations affect how readers interpret evidence.

items.title: Scatterplots
items.text: Define scatterplots in relation to relationship visualization; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

items.title: Regression plots
items.text: Work through regression plots using a small, synthetic example before scaling up. State what the calculation or method returns and why that result is useful.

items.title: Correlation heatmaps
items.text: Check the edge cases for correlation heatmaps: missing values, unusual ranges, different groups, time boundaries, or a changed input can affect the conclusion.

items.title: Pair plots
items.text: Document the rule or choice for pair plots so another learner can reproduce the analysis and understand its limitations.

items.title: Bubble charts
items.text: Define bubble charts in relation to relationship visualization; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Restate the question addressed by relationship visualization. 2. Identify the input data, intended output, and assumptions. 3. Predict what the small example should show before reading its output. 4. Change one input or assumption, compare the result, and document what remains uncertain.

content_blocks.run_instructions: For Python, copy the snippet into a local file and run with Python 3. This CodeLeaf block is static and does not execute inside the browser. For SQL, adapt the query to an approved local schema; the stated result is a conceptual query simulation, not a live database result.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the provided synthetic input, rerun or retrace the example, and change one value at a time. Do not use personal records, credentials, or data you are not authorized to access.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Keep the question, data grain, units, and assumptions explicit. If a result differs, inspect the input and steps in order. Avoid turning an observed association into a causal claim, treating a sample as the population, or assuming a small demonstration guarantees production behavior. Summaries and charts complement each other; do not conceal distributions behind a single number.

content_blocks.title: Responsible interpretation
content_blocks.text: This example is a teaching aid. It is static in the CodeLeaf lesson and is not executed in the browser. It uses small synthetic values; validate any real workflow in a separate, appropriate local environment and protect sensitive data.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: A visualization encodes values using position, length, area, color, and other channels. The chart type, axis, units, ordering, and annotations affect how readers interpret evidence. Next, connect this lesson to the linked prerequisite or following lesson. Record the method, input assumptions, observed result, and one limitation so another person can reproduce and review the work.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small synthetic example for relationship visualization. State a question, make a prediction, trace or run an appropriate calculation, then write one finding and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: Refer accurately to the topic and its syllabus subtopics.
Record a reproducible example or a complete manual trace with an expected result.
Document at least one assumption, limitation, data-quality issue, or evaluation check.
hints: Write down the input, expected result, units, and assumptions first.
Change only one condition when testing a revised example.
Ask whether the data and method represent the real decision; do not infer causality or production readiness from a toy example.
troubleshooting: Check input values, path assumptions, package versions, indentation, and units.
For SQL, use a local schema and read-only test data; this page does not provide a live database.
For package-dependent work, create an isolated environment and use the relevant official documentation.
